metadata.description: Can the learner tell a specific, useful request from a vague one?

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: A note written to sound as angry as possible may make the problem harder to solve. Ask for a clear, polite note that states the problem and the change you want.
This request says who the note is for, what the problem is, when it happens, and what you want. It also sets the tone. Specific detail like this is what lets a tool give you a draft you can use.
With no goal, tone or details, the tool has to guess what you want. You are likely to get something generic that you cannot use. Say what the note is for and what should happen.

This gives a goal and a tone, which is good, but leaves out the details that make the note useful. You can add them afterward, so some people would accept it. It works better to put the key facts in the first request.
connections.notes: Ambiguous on purpose: the plan is workable, but a stronger request exists.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Leaving the number out avoids the risk, and for a casual chat that may be fine. But if the figure matters to your point, checking it is the better move.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: safe, but gives up the information instead of verifying it.

connections.feedback: Asking the same tool if it is sure is not an independent check. It can say yes to a wrong answer. Go back to the original source.
Confident wording does not prove a number is right. Check the figure in the original article or another source you trust before you repeat it.
A clear, confident tone is not evidence. AI summaries can change or invent details while still sounding sure. Check the number first.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Trace the figure to the original article or another source you trust. In work, others will rely on it, so checking comes before sharing.
Leaving the figure out removes the risk, which may suit a short note. If the number supports your argument, though, a quick check lets you keep it.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: reasonable when the number is not central.

connections.feedback: A well-written summary can still contain a wrong or invented number. Others will rely on what you share, so check it first.
Saying an AI tool wrote the summary is honest, but it does not make the number correct. You should still check the figure before you pass it on.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Made-up rows with the same columns are a smart way to get help without exposing real data. But you still need to know your workplace rules first, so some would rank the policy step ahead of it.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: a good technique, but it skips the first step of checking the rules.

connections.feedback: Formatting help still means the private details leave your control. The task being simple does not make the data safe to share.
Checking facts is a good habit, but it does not solve this problem. The risk here is sharing private customer details, not whether the output is accurate.
Customers' details are private. First learn what your workplace allows, then remove or replace names, numbers and notes before using any outside tool.

connections.feedback: Names are not facts, so there is little to check. A quick search to see whether a name is already used nearby is sensible, though. Reasonable people could disagree on whether this counts as the best first move.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: the same answer is strong or incorrect in other sets; here it is only partly relevant.

connections.feedback: Not everything AI suggests is copied. Familiar words can show up, so a quick search is wise, but you can still use the list as inspiration.
The order of a list does not mean the first item is best. AI has no special reason for putting it first. Look at several and choose.
A list of ideas is a starting point. You pick, change and decide. This is a good use of AI because mistakes cost little.

origin.author: READY builder
origin.source_reference: Original draft material; not an official assessment; awaiting owner review

connections.feedback: Writing it yourself from the real procedure and using AI only for wording is also careful. Both routes keep a person in charge, so it comes down to which fits your team.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: a reasonable alternative that keeps accuracy with the author.

connections.feedback: The tool cannot verify your workplace's procedures, and it may agree with a flawed notice. Review by someone who knows the facts is what counts.
AI can speed up a first draft, but safety details must be right. A person who knows the procedures should check each line, and you remain responsible for what goes out.
Being asked to use AI does not move responsibility to the tool. An unchecked safety notice could contain mistakes that hurt someone.

connections.feedback: A teacher stays responsible for what students receive, whoever or whatever drafted it.
AI can reflect patterns in its training that treat some styles or backgrounds less fairly. Reviewing feedback helps you catch and correct that.
AI tools can usually read much more than a sentence. The real reasons to review are about meaning and fairness, not length.
AI works from the words on the page. It can misread what a student meant, so a teacher should check that feedback fits the real work.

connections.feedback: Last week's update says nothing about this week's progress. The tool would be guessing, and a guess is not a report.
The tool does not know what happened this week. Comparing the draft with your own notes keeps the update accurate.
A request that already works gives a similar result each time and saves effort. Keep it and adjust the details each week.
Private messages may contain information that should not be shared. Give the tool only the notes you need for the update.

connections.feedback: A checklist is useful, but handed over without an example it may not change the belief. Many coaches would pair the two.
connections.notes: Ambiguous: a helpful step that works better after a demonstration.

connections.feedback: People often learn best from seeing it happen. A real example with a mistake, and how you caught it, shows why checking matters without a lecture.
AI does not work like a calculator that follows fixed rules. It produces likely-sounding text, which can be wrong.
Telling someone they are wrong ends the conversation without teaching anything. Showing them is more persuasive.
